title: Govinda

teacherSummary.text: Old Govinda, still searching, comes to the ferry and asks for teaching. Siddhartha says that wisdom cannot be communicated in words, that every truth's opposite is also true, and that one must love the world. Asked to kiss Siddhartha's forehead, Govinda sees in his face a stream of countless faces and forms—the unity of all things—and bows, weeping, before his friend's smile.

vocabulary.definition: A sight or view of the interior of anything
vocabulary.context: But haven’t you found something by yourself, though you’ve found no teachings, you still found certain thoughts, certain insights, which are your own and which help you to live?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: Having a disposition to do good
vocabulary.context: The face was unchanged, after under its surface the depth of the thousandfoldness had closed up again, he smiled silently, smiled quietly and softly, perhaps very benevolently, perhaps very mockingly, precisely as he used to smile, the exalted one.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: One who, or that which, searhes or examines
vocabulary.context: Aren’t you too, ferryman, a searcher for the right path?”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.context: (But secretly he thought to himself: This Siddhartha is a bizarre person, he expresses bizarre thoughts, his teachings sound foolish.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.context: It is not possible for any person to see how far another one has already progressed on his path; in the robber and dice-gambler, the Buddha is waiting; in the Brahmin, the robber is waiting.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: The power or capacity of enduring
vocabulary.context: He commands benevolence, clemency, sympathy, tolerance, but not love; he forbade us to tie our heart in love to earthly things.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: Existing, happening, or done, at the same time
vocabulary.context: In deep meditation, there is the possibility to put time out of existence, to see all life which was, is, and will be as if it was simultaneous, and there everything is good, everything is perfect, everything is Brahman.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: The act of clothing with flesh, or the state of being so clothed
vocabulary.context: It is unlikely for one of us to see the other again in this incarnation.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.context: But most of all, I have learned here from this river and from my predecessor, the ferryman Vasudeva.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: To free from that which infolds or envelops
vocabulary.context: The sinner is not on his way to become a Buddha, he is not in the process of developing, though our capacity for thinking does not know how else to picture these things.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

context.history: The ending echoes Buddhist ideas of non-self and the Hindu idea of the oneness of reality.

significance: The final image, Siddhartha's smile resembling Gotama's, suggests he has found his own path to enlightenment.
discussionQuestions: Govinda followed a teacher all his life; Siddhartha followed experience. Who learned more?
Where does theme appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with experience versus teaching?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Govinda,” how does Hesse show wisdom cannot be taught? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the theme you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Govinda develops the idea of wisdom cannot be taught. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of theme and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Hermann Hesse uses theme in Govinda to complicate the reader's understanding of wisdom cannot be taught. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Govinda within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of wisdom cannot be taught responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Govinda as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of wisdom cannot be taught. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Siddhartha.

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: Govinda followed a teacher all his life; Siddhartha followed experience. Who learned more? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include insights, benevolently, searcher, bizarre, progressed. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “But haven’t you found something by yourself, though you’ve found no teachings, you still found certain thoughts, certain insights, which are your own and which help you to live?” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: A sight or view of the interior of anything.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Siddhartha would have known. The ending echoes Buddhist ideas of non-self and the Hindu idea of the oneness of reality. Now, why does this chapter matter? The final image, Siddhartha's smile resembling Gotama's, suggests he has found his own path to enlightenment. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Theme, Characterization, Irony.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot theme, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
